svg.title: Azure Local private path
svg.desc: Azure Local non-bypassed HTTPS enters the host Arc proxy. Gateway-supported HTTPS uses the Arc gateway tunnel. Other required public-endpoint HTTPS uses Azure Firewall explicit proxy without Arc gateway. The dotted gold path shows non-bypassed machine OS HTTP going from the host through the enterprise firewall and private connection to Azure Firewall explicit proxy, then to permitted public endpoints. HTTP does not enter Arc proxy or Arc gateway. Private endpoint traffic outside gateway coverage uses a direct connection from Arc proxy over the private network, not Azure Firewall explicit proxy. Packet motion is continuous and illustrative. Reduced-motion preferences hide moving packets. Direct intranet traffic leaves the Azure Local machine before the Arc proxy. The solid teal machine-side bypass line branches before the enterprise firewall: the local branch stays entirely on-premises and reaches intranet DNS, Active Directory, file services, and monitoring systems. This local route uses the appropriate service protocols, not an HTTP proxy or an Azure tunnel. It does not cross the enterprise firewall, ExpressRoute or VPN, Azure Firewall explicit proxy, or Arc gateway in this schematic. The generic Private endpoints component has two alternative access paths. The solid teal branch illustrates explicit proxy bypass: traffic crosses the enterprise firewall as network transit and uses ExpressRoute or site-to-site VPN to reach a private IP inside the Azure virtual network, without entering either proxy or Arc gateway. The dashed teal branch starts at Arc proxy, which connects directly to the private endpoint for destinations outside Arc gateway coverage. The enterprise firewall and private connection provide network transit only; this path never enters Azure Firewall explicit proxy or Arc gateway and needs no bypass-list entry. The two paths terminate at the same generic component to compare routing options, not to require both paths for each request. Private DNS resolution on the host and permitted network access to the private IP are still required. The blue highlighted path is the Arc gateway HTTP CONNECT tunnel. It starts at the host Arc proxy, passes through the enterprise firewall, ExpressRoute or site-to-site VPN, and Azure Firewall explicit proxy, and terminates at the Arc gateway public endpoint. Supported HTTPS travels inside this tunnel; the explicit proxy forwards it without TLS inspection. The gateway then forwards to Microsoft-managed Azure services. Arc gateway and Azure services are grouped in the Azure backbone area, separate from third-party endpoints on the public internet. The rose path carries other required public-endpoint HTTPS through the same private transport and explicit proxy without traversing the Arc gateway. It reaches non-gateway Azure public endpoints or third-party internet destinations, not private endpoints. The shaded tunnel is a logical connection, not a separate network resource or a Private Link endpoint.
svg.text: Host traffic, intranet services, and Private Link

path.title: Non-bypassed machine OS HTTPS enters the host Arc proxy.

Non-bypassed machine OS HTTP goes from the Azure Local host through the enterprise firewall and ExpressRoute or site-to-site VPN to Azure Firewall explicit proxy. It does not enter the host Arc proxy, cluster IP proxy, or Arc gateway. The firewall and private connection provide network transit.

Azure Firewall explicit proxy forwards permitted HTTP to the required public endpoints. This path branches to Azure public services or continues to third-party internet endpoints; it does not use Arc gateway or private endpoints.
The explicit proxy forwards permitted HTTP to a required Azure public endpoint. The Azure-services component groups destinations; each service determines which protocols its endpoints accept.
Arc gateway HTTP CONNECT tunnel: host Arc proxy to the public Arc gateway, carried through the enterprise firewall, ExpressRoute or site-to-site VPN, and Azure Firewall explicit proxy.
The Arc gateway forwards gateway-supported HTTPS to Microsoft-managed Azure services.

Required public-endpoint HTTPS outside Arc gateway coverage uses the enterprise firewall, private connection, and Azure Firewall explicit proxy. Its branches reach Azure public services or third-party internet endpoints, not private endpoints.
Required Azure endpoints not supported by Arc gateway are reached directly through Azure Firewall explicit proxy on the Azure backbone, not through the third-party public-internet area.

For private endpoint FQDNs outside Arc gateway coverage, Arc proxy connects directly to the endpoint private IP. The enterprise firewall and ExpressRoute or site-to-site VPN provide network transit only. This path does not enter Azure Firewall explicit proxy or Arc gateway and needs no bypass-list entry. It is distinct from the solid teal host-side bypass because it starts at Arc proxy. Host private DNS resolution and permitted network access are required.

Direct connection from the Azure Local machine to the private endpoint IP in the VNet. The enterprise firewall and ExpressRoute or site-to-site VPN provide network transit only. This route completely bypasses the Arc proxy, Arc gateway, and Azure Firewall explicit proxy.

Local branch of the direct machine-side bypass line, before the enterprise firewall. Traffic to on-premises DNS, Active Directory, file services, and monitoring stays local and does not enter Arc proxy, enterprise firewall, ExpressRoute or VPN, Azure Firewall explicit proxy, or Arc gateway in this schematic.

g.text: Direct Private Link from Arc proxy; no bypass entry
